# Introduction

This document walks through the full bioregionalisation workflow for the
**Aegean Islands**, integrating taxonomic and phylogenetic beta
diversity, hierarchical clustering, statistical validation, indicator
species analysis, V-measure comparison and Generalized Dissimilarity
Modelling (GDM). All analyses are reproducible — every intermediate
object is cached in `RDS/` and every figure exported to `results/`. You
can find and download everything we will do in this workshop from its
Github repository:
[Botany_Upatras_2026](https://github.com/kkougiou/Botany_Upatras_2026).

## Aegean Islands shapefile

Let's load a shapefile with the 48 Aegean islands included in our
dataset.

```{r aegean-islands}
##============================================================================##
## Load the Aegean Islands shapefile ----
##============================================================================##
aegean_islands <- read_sf("Shapefiles/Aegean Islands.shp") %>% 
  
  ## Change the CRS to Greek grid to calculate the area of each island
  st_transform(2100) %>% 
  
  ## Create a new column named Area
  dplyr::mutate(Area = as.numeric(st_area(.))/ 1e6) %>% 
  
  ## Change the CRS back to WGS84
  st_transform(4326)
##============================================================================##
```

## Abiotic data

We will load 63 abiotic variables, which I have preprocessed to save us
some time.

First, I assembled a high-resolution (1 km) monthly climate dataset for
2015, comprising 19 WorldClim bioclimatic variables (Fick and Hijmans
2017) and 16 additional environmental variables [@title_envirem_2018].

I selected 2015 as the baseline year to ensure temporal compatibility
across all abiotic predictors.

The 1 km resolution represents a pragmatic compromise between capturing
environmentally meaningful heterogeneity and maintaining computational
tractability and is considered appropriate for modelling distributions
of these relatively range-restricted endemic taxa.

Altitude data from the `CGIAR Consortium for Spatial Information`
[@jarvis_hole-filled_2008-1], underpinned the dataset, which I processed
using `ClimateEU` v4.63, together with the R packages `dismo` 1.1.4
[@hijmans_dismo_2017] and `envirem` 2.2 [@title_envirem_2018], following
established protocols [@wang_climatewnahigh-resolution_2012;
@hamann_comprehensive_2013; @marchi_climateeu_2020].

Specifically, I fed the altitudinal data into `ClimateEU`v4.63 to
generate monthly climate surfaces, from which I derived 37 climatic
variables using the functions `biovars`, `ETsolradRasters`, and
`generateEnvirem` from the `dismo` and `envirem` packages.

Temporally dynamic land use data originated from [@chen_global_2022],
who produced global land use projections at 1 km resolution. The
original dataset comprises 20 land use categories, which I converted
into separate binary predictors. To reduce multicollinearity and improve
model parsimony, I consolidated the 20 categories into six broader,
ecologically meaningful classes: 'forests', 'shrubs', 'grasslands',
'barren', 'crops', and 'urban'. I performed this aggregation using the
`terra` 1.7.46 [@hijmans_terra_2023] R package. For each aggregated
class, I then generated continuous raster layers of Euclidean distance
using the `distance` function from the same package, thereby capturing
edge effects and spatial proximity to specific land-cover types.

I further incorporated soil metrics from SoilGrids
[@hengl_soilgrids250m_2017], resampled where necessary to match the 1 km
resolution of the remaining predictors.

Five topographical metrics, `aspect`, `heat load index`, `slope`,
`topographic position index`, and `terrain ruggedness index`, were
computed from the altitude data using functions in the R packages
`terra` 1.7.46 (Hijmans 2023) and `spatialEco` 1.2-0
[@evans_spatialeco_2019].

I also obtained rainfall soil erosivity data developed by Panagos et al.
[@panagos_global_2023] and made available from the European Soil Data
Centre [@panagos_european_2012; @panagos_european_2022], resampled to
the same spatial resolution. Soil hydraulic properties, including
`field capacity`, `moisture retention curve`, `saturated water content`,
`wilting point`, `saturated hydraulic connectivity`, and
`hydraulic conductivity curve` [@toth_3d_2017], were integrated into the
environmental dataset at consistent resolution.

Additionally, I retrieved geomorphological, geological, hydrological,
lithological, and soil richness data at 1 km resolution from Toivanen et
al. [-@toivanen2024geodiversity].

Finally, as a measure of human impact, I obtained Global Human
Modification Index data from Kennedy et al. [-@kennedy_managing_2019]
retaining the same spatial resolution as the other abiotic data.

```{r abiotic-data, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Load the abiotic data ----
##============================================================================##
abiotic <- rast('Rasters/Current abiotic variables.tif')
abiotic
```

## Median abiotic values per island

We will now extract all abiotic data at the island level and calculate
their median value using the `exactextract` function from the
`exactextractr` 0.10.1 R package [@baston_package_2021].

```{r median-abiotic}
##============================================================================##
## Create a dataframe with the median values for all the abiotic data in each island ----
##============================================================================##
exact_lulc <- exact_extract(abiotic,
                            
                            ## We need to convert the SpatVector to an sf object
                            ## for the exact_extract function to work properly
                            aegean_islands,
                            
                            ## We want the median value for each abiotic
                            ## variable and island
                            'median') %>% 
  
  ## We create a new column named Island based on the island names from our
  ## dataframe
  dplyr::mutate(Island = aegean_islands$Island) %>% 
  
  ## We move the newly created column to the beginning of the dataframe 
  dplyr::select(Island, everything()) %>% 
  as_tibble() %>%
  
  ## We remove the "median." prefix from the column names to make them more
  ## readable
  rename_with(~ str_remove(., "^median\\."), 
              starts_with("median.")) %>% 
  
  full_join(., 
            
            ## Calculate the Maximum distance between each island pair
            apply((st_distance(aegean_islands %>% st_centroid(), 
                         aegean_islands %>% st_centroid()) / 1e+3) %>% 
              as_tibble() %>% 
              set_names(aegean_islands$Island) %>% 
              units::drop_units() %>% 
              mutate(across(everything(), ~ na_if(.x, 0))),
              1,
              max, 
              na.rm = T) %>% 
  enframe() %>% 
  rename(MaxD = value) %>% 
  mutate(Island = aegean_islands$Island) %>% 
  dplyr::select(Island, MaxD) %>%
  
  full_join(., 
            
            ## Calculate the Minimum distance between each island pair
            apply((st_distance(aegean_islands %>% 
                                 st_centroid(), 
                               aegean_islands %>% 
                                 st_centroid())/1e+3) %>% 
                    as_tibble() %>% 
                    set_names(aegean_islands$Island) %>% 
                    units::drop_units() %>% 
                    mutate(across(everything(), ~ na_if(.x, 0))),
                  1, 
                  min, 
                  na.rm = T) %>% 
              enframe() %>% 
              rename(MinD = value) %>% 
              mutate(Island = aegean_islands$Island) %>% 
              dplyr::select(Island, MinD))) %>% 
  
  ## We join the dataframe with the median values for each island with the
  ## original shapefile to create a new sf object that contains both the median
  ## values and the geometry of the islands
  left_join(aegean_islands, ., by = "Island") 

exact_lulc 
##============================================================================##
```

```{r load-slow-file-exact, include = FALSE, cache = TRUE, eval = T}
exact_lulc <- readRDS('RDS/Median values for the abiotic data for the Aegean islands.rds')
```

```{r save-lulc}
##============================================================================##
## Save it to disk ----
##============================================================================##
saveRDS(exact_lulc,
        'RDS/Median values for the abiotic data for the Aegean islands.rds')
##============================================================================##

```

## Collinearity filtering

We will filter our initial set of 63 abiotic predictors to prevent
collinearity and model overfitting. To this end, we will use the
function `collinear` from the `collinear` 3.0.0 R package
[@benito_collinear_2023]. We will centre and scale all variables prior
to modelling and remove any variables exhibiting zero and near zero
variance using the `preProcess` function from the `caret` 7.0.1 R
package [@kuhn_building_2008], as well as the variables with pairwise
Spearman rank correlations and variance inflation factors equal to or
above 0.7 and 2.5, respectively [@dormann_correlation_2012].

```{r collinearity-filter, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Collinearity filtering ----
##============================================================================##
env_data <- exact_lulc %>% 
  st_drop_geometry()

env_cols <- setdiff(names(env_data), "Island")

# A) Remove variables with zero variance (values that are the same everywhere)
env_preprocessed <- env_data %>%
  select(all_of(env_cols)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  {\(df) predict(preProcess(df, method = c("zv", "nzv", 
                                           "corr", "center",
                                           "scale")), df)}()

# B) Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) filtering
uncorr_env <- collinear(
  df      = env_preprocessed,
  max_cor = 0.7,    # drop pairs with |r| > 0.7
  max_vif = 2.5     # drop variables with VIF > 2.5
)$result$df %>%
  mutate(Island = env_data$Island) %>%
  select(Island, everything()) %>%
  as_tibble()

uncorr_env
```

# Phylogeny construction

Let's construct a phylogenetic tree for the taxa occurring in these 48
Aegean islands.

## Unique taxa

```{r taxa-list, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Get the unique taxa for which to create the phylogeny ----
##============================================================================##
taxa <- plants %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = -Island,
    names_to  = "Taxon", 
    values_to = "presence"
  ) %>% 
  distinct(Taxon)
##============================================================================##
```

## Megatree & phylogenetic tree

```{r build-phylogeny}
##============================================================================##
## Pre-load the megatree ----
##============================================================================##
mega_tree <- megatrees::tree_plant_otl
##============================================================================##

##============================================================================##
## Create the phylogenetic tree ----
##============================================================================##
phy <- get_tree(taxa$Taxon,
                taxon    = 'plant',
                scenario = "random_below_basal")

saveRDS(phy, 'RDS/Phylogenetic tree for the Aegean taxa.rds')
##============================================================================##
```

```{r load-slow-file-phy, include = FALSE, cache = TRUE, eval = T}
phy <- readRDS('RDS/Phylogenetic tree for the Aegean taxa.rds')
```

## Match community matrix to phylogeny

```{r match-comm-phy, eval = T, results = 'hide'}
##============================================================================##
## Create the community matrices and the phylogeny ----
##============================================================================##
comm <- picante::match.phylo.comm(phy, 
                                  plants %>% 
                                    as.data.frame())$comm
phy  <- picante::match.phylo.comm(phy, 
                                  plants %>% 
                                    as.data.frame())$phy

## Save it to disk if you want by removing the #
# saveRDS(comm, 'RDS/Community matrix for the Aegean taxa.rds')

rownames(comm) <- plants$Island
##============================================================================##
```

## Sparse / dense conversion

```{r prepare-comm, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Prepare the community matrix ----
##============================================================================##
if (!inherits(comm, "dgCMatrix")) {
  comm_sparse <- Matrix(as.matrix(comm), sparse = TRUE)
} else {
  comm_sparse <- comm
}

# Convert to a dense presence/absence matrix
if (inherits(comm_sparse, "sparseMatrix")) {
  comm_dense <- as.matrix(comm_sparse)
} else {
  comm_dense <- as.matrix(comm)
}

# Ensure strict presence/absence
comm_dense[comm_dense > 0] <- 1
storage.mode(comm_dense) <- "integer"
##============================================================================##
```

# Alpha diversity

## Biodiversity metrics

Let's calculate several biodiversity metrics for the 48 Aegean islands
in our dataset:

-   Species richness (SR)
-   Weighted endemism (CWE)
-   Phylogenetic diversity (PD)
-   Phylogenetic endemism (PE)
-   Phylogenetic diversity standardized for species richness (PD_SES)

```{r biodiversity metrics, tidy = F, eval = T}
sr <- plants %>% 
  
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -Island,
    names_to = "Taxon", 
    values_to = "presence"
  ) %>% 
  
  ## Keep only the presences
  dplyr::filter(presence == 1) %>% 
  
  ## Find out how many taxa are present in each island
  dplyr::count(Island) %>% 
  
  ## Arrange them in descending order
  arrange(desc(n)) %>% 
  dplyr::rename(SR = n,
                Island = Island) %>% 
  
  ## Arrange them by alphabetical order
  arrange(Island) %>% 
  
  ## Create the rest biodiversity metrics
  dplyr::mutate(WE = weighted_endemism(comm_sparse),
                PD = PD(comm_sparse, phy),
                PE = phylo_endemism(comm_sparse, phy),
                PD_SES = PD_ses(comm_sparse, 
                                phy,
                                reps = 100, 
                                model = 'tipshuffle')$pd_obs.z,
                PD_SES_p_value = PD_ses(comm_sparse,
                                        phy, 
                                        reps = 100, 
                                        model = 'tipshuffle')$pd_pvalue) %>% 
  
  ## Join them with the abiotic and spatial data
  left_join(exact_lulc,
            ., 
            by = "Island") 

## Simple plot
plot(sr['SR'])
plot(sr['WE'])
plot(sr['PD'])
plot(sr['PE'])
plot(sr['PD_SES'])
```

```{r sr-slow-file, include = FALSE, cache = TRUE, eval = T}
sr <- readRDS('RDS/SR.rds')
```

## Hotspots & Coldspots

We can easily identify the biodiversity hotspots & coldspots for every
metric we calculated, as well for a combination of those metrics (e.g.,
WE-PE).

```{r WEPE}

sr <- sr %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(
                ## Calculate the top 5% hotspots
                HT_5_WE = hotspots(WE, prob = 5),
                HT_5_PE = hotspots(PE, prob = 5),
                HT_5_SR = hotspots(SR, prob = 5),
                HT_5_PD = hotspots(PD, prob = 5),
                
                ## Calculate the top 5% coldspots
                CT_5_WE = coldspots(WE, prob = 5),
                CT_5_PE = coldspots(PE, prob = 5),
                CT_5_SR = coldspots(SR, prob = 5),
                CT_5_PD = coldspots(PD, prob = 5),
                
                ## Calculate the hotspot and coldspot intersection
                HT_5_WEPE = HT_5_WE * HT_5_PE,
                CT_5_WEPE = CT_5_WE * CT_5_PE,
                
                ## For easier visualisation
                we_pe_hot = ifelse(HT_5_WE == 1 & HT_5_PE == 1,
                                    'HOT',
                                    ifelse(CT_5_WE == 1 & CT_5_PE == 1, 
                                           'COLD', 
                                           'Neither')))
```

```{r sr vis, eval = T}
## Quick visualisation
sr %>% 
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = we_pe_hot)) + 
  labs(title = 'Diversity hotspots in the Aegean') + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('steelblue1','red', 'gray90'),
                    name = "Diversity hotspots",
                    labels = c("COLD", "HOT", "Neither")) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

```

> Create the top-1 & top-10 hotspots & coldspots and then plot them

## **Species - Area relationship**\*

It's considered one of the few ecological laws, as it applies to all
taxonomic entities.

![](G:/Academic/Lessons/EMB/Labs/Labs/Figures%20for%20Labs/1.png)

Simply put, the larger the area, the more species it can support. This
relationship is often expressed mathematically as:

![](G:/Academic/Lessons/EMB/Labs/Labs/Figures%20for%20Labs/2.png)

![](G:/Academic/Lessons/EMB/Labs/Labs/Figures%20for%20Labs/3.png)

![](G:/Academic/Lessons/EMB/Labs/Labs/Figures%20for%20Labs/4.png)

There aer however many other abiotic variables (e.g., climate,
topography, geology, soil) that can influence the patterns of species
diversity and distribution in space and time.

![](G:/Academic/Lessons/EMB/Labs/Labs/Figures%20for%20Labs/5.png)

![](G:/Academic/Lessons/EMB/Labs/Labs/Figures%20for%20Labs/6.png)

In many macroecological analyses, apart from a select few that are
indifferent to collinearity, homoscedacity and other statistical
assumptions (e.g., Random Forests), we need to center, scaleand filter
our abiotic predictors to prevent model overfitting and ensure the
interpretability of our results when dealing with SARs. Thankfully,
we've already done that in a prior step (see the Collinearity section
above). So we can go on and use our dataset.

### **Model creation - ISAR**

We are now able to create 2 simple linear regression models, one for
taxonomic and one for phylogenetic diversity in relation to area:

```{r ISAR, eval = TRUE}
##============================================================================##
## First create the ISAR dataset from the filtered IVs and the biodiversity metrics
##============================================================================##
srdf <- uncorr_env %>% 
  full_join(., sr %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              dplyr::select(Island, SR:CT_5_WEPE)) %>% 
  dplyr::select(Island, everything())
##============================================================================##


##============================================================================##
## Then define the predictors
##============================================================================##
aegean_predictors <- sr %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  dplyr::select(any_of(colnames(uncorr_env))) %>% 
  dplyr::select(-Island) %>% 
  colnames()
##============================================================================##


##============================================================================##
## ISAR models
##============================================================================##
model1 <- lm(SR ~ Area, data = srdf)
model2 <- lm(PD ~ Area, data = srdf)
model3 <- lm(WE ~ Area, data = srdf)
model4 <- lm(PE ~ Area, data = srdf)
##============================================================================##
```

### **Model summary**

Let's see what we've got

```{r model1, eval = TRUE}
##============================================================================##
## Check the summary
##============================================================================##
summary(model1)
```

```{r model2, eval = TRUE}
##============================================================================##
## Check the summary
##============================================================================##
summary(model2)
```

**Attention** We're interested in the *adjusted R squared*

> Do the same for the other 2 models

### **Standardized residuals creation**

Let's now create the standardized residuals for both models, which will
be used to identify the islands that are hotspots (positive residuals)
and coldspots (negative residuals) of taxonomic and phylogenetic
diversity, respectively, after controlling for area.

```{r rstandard, eval = TRUE}
##============================================================================##
## Create the residuals
##============================================================================##
res_sr <- rstandard(model1)
res_pd <- rstandard(model2)
##============================================================================##
```

> Do it for the other two models as well

**We can do all this in one single step**

```{r metrics, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Check the estimate and the p-value
##============================================================================##
metrics <- lm(SR ~ Area, data = srdf) %>%
  broom::tidy() %>% 
  full_join(., lm(PD ~ Area, data = srdf) %>% 
              broom::tidy()) %>% 
  mutate(Metric = rep(c('SR','PD'), each = 2)) %>% 
  dplyr::select(Metric, everything())

metrics

##============================================================================##
## Check the metrics
##============================================================================##
metrics <- lm(SR ~ Area, data = srdf) %>% 
  broom::glance() %>% 
  full_join(., lm(PD ~ Area, data = srdf) %>% 
              broom::glance()) %>% 
  mutate(Metric = c('SR','PD')) %>% 
  dplyr::select(Metric, everything())

metrics


##============================================================================##
## Check the residuals
##============================================================================##
resids <- lm(SR ~ Area, 
             data = srdf) %>% 
  broom::augment() %>% 
  mutate(Island = srdf$Island)  %>% 
  rename(SR_res = .std.resid) %>% 
  full_join(., lm(PD ~ Area, data = srdf) %>% 
              broom::augment() %>% 
              mutate(Island = srdf$Island) %>% 
              rename(PD_res = .std.resid),
            by = 'Island') %>% 
  dplyr::select(Island, SR, SR_res, PD, PD_res)

resids
```

> Try adding the other two models as well

### **Scatterplot**

We will now create a scatterplot to see which island constitutes a
hotspot of plant diversity for the total number of plant taxa (SR), as
well as for PD:

```{r scatteplot, eval=TRUE, fig.cap='Scatterplot of the 48 Aegean islands', fig.height=10, fig.width=10, warning=FALSE}

## Plot

ggplot(srdf, aes(res_sr, res_pd)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = Island), 
            fontface = "bold", 
            size = 2.8, 
            vjust = -1.2, 
            hjust = 0.5) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.0) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.0) + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  xlab(expression(bold("SR"))) + 
  ylab(expression(bold("PD"))) 
```

### **A variety of ISAR models**

There are 20 models trying to explain the species-area relationship,
which differ in the way they model the relationship between species
richness and area (e.g., linear, logarithmic, power, etc.). We can use
the `sars` 0.1.0 R package to fit all these models and compare their
performance using AICc.The authors of the `sars` package have written a
detailed and thorough paper explaining the different models and their
assumptions, which I highly recommend reading if you want to learn more
about this topic.

Let's dive in.

```{r sars, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Prepare data for Species Richness (SR) ----
##============================================================================##

# sars' strictly requires a 2-column dataframe: Area (1st) and Metric (2nd)
isar_data_sr <- sr %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  dplyr::select(Area, SR) %>% 
  as.data.frame()

isar_data_sr
```

```{r sars2, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Fit a Single Classic Model 
##============================================================================##
# The classic Arrhenius Power Model: S = c * A^z
fit_power <- sar_power(isar_data_sr)

# Check the summary (gives you the c and z parameters, R-squared, etc.)
summary(fit_power)

plot(fit_power)
```

If the following function throw any warnings, fear not. These warnings
are completely normal when running non-linear models (Non-linear Least
Squares). Certain mathematical functions (such as the Gompertz or
Chapman) are overly complex for the shape of our data. The algorithm
manages to fit the line, but it struggles to calculate the standard
errors (parameter statistics). The great thing about the Multi-Model
approach is that we don't need to worry: the AICc will assign near-zero
weight (Akaike weight = 0) to these unstable models, practically
eliminating them from the final averaged curve.

```{r sars3, eval = F}
##============================================================================##
## Multiple ISAR models ----
##============================================================================##

# This function fits up to 20 different ISAR models (Power, Exponential, 
# Logarithmic, Asymptotic, etc.), calculates their AICc, and averages them

# Note: It might throw warnings if some complex models fail to converge on your 
# specific data points, but it will automatically drop the failed ones.

# We run the sar_average WITHOUT strict residual filtering.
# Ecological data rarely have perfectly normal residuals. Instead of arbitrarily 
# rejecting models, we rely on Information Theory (AICc) to down-weight poor fits.

fit_avg <- sar_average(data = isar_data_sr,
                       crit = "Info",            # Automatically switches to AICc
                       grid_start = "partial",   # Robust parameter search
                       normaTest = "none",       # RELAXED: Do not reject models based on normality
                       homoTest = "none",        # RELAXED: Do not reject models based on homoscedasticity
                       confInt = TRUE, 
                       ciN = 50,                ## It should be set to 1000 for publication-quality results, but it takes a long time to run.
                       verb = TRUE)              # Show progress and warnings in the console
```

> **Conceptual Note: Why did we set `normaTest = "none"`?**
>
> In macroecology, empirical data (like species counts and island areas)
> are inherently noisy and rarely produce perfectly normally distributed
> residuals. If we applied strict frequentist filters (like the
> Shapiro-Wilk test), almost all ISAR models would be rejected, leaving
> us with no tools to analyze our data.
>
> Instead of binary rejection (pass/fail), the modern approach uses
> **Information Theory (AICc)**. We retain all models and let the Akaike
> Weights ($w_i$) naturally penalize and down-weight the models that fit
> the data poorly. This way, we can still extract meaningful insights
> from the data without arbitrarily discarding models based on strict
> assumptions that are often violated in real-world ecological datasets.

```{r load-slow-file-sars, include = FALSE, cache = TRUE, eval = T}
fit_avg <- readRDS('RDS/isar_multimodel_fit.rds')
```

```{r sars5, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Explore the results ----
##============================================================================##

# Which SAR models performed best (ranked by their Akaike weights)
summary(fit_avg)
```

> **Conceptual Note: Model Shape and Asymptotes**
>
> Not all Species-Area curves look the same. Look at the summary of your
> individual SAR models (or the output of `sar_average()$details`).
>
> **Convex-up:** Richness increases rapidly at first, then slows down,
> but never truly stops growing.
>
> **Asymptotic:** The curve eventually flattens completely into a
> horizontal line. Biologically, this implies the island has reached
> maximum "saturation" or the entire regional species pool has been
> sampled[^1].
>
> **Question:** Based on the weights of the asymptotic models (e.g.,
> `Asymp`, `Gompertz`, `Logistic`) versus the non-asymptotic ones (e.g.,
> `Power`, `Logarithmic`) in our Aegean dataset, does the Aegean flora
> exhibit signs of strict saturation?

[^1]: Whether an archipelago reaches an asymptote (i.e., it ceases to
    add new species regardless of how much the area increases) indicates
    that the system has reached its carrying capacity or that the
    regional species pool has been exhausted.

```{r sars6, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Plot ----
##============================================================================##
# This plot will show the individual models as thin lines, and the final 
# Weighted Average Model as a thick, prominent line.

par(mfrow = c(3,1)) 

#plot all model fits and the multimodel SAR curve as a separate curve on top
plot(fit_avg, 
     ModTitle = "a) Multimodel SAR",
     mmSep = TRUE)

#plot the multimodel SAR curve (with confidence intervals) on its own 
plot(fit_avg, allCurves = FALSE, ModTitle =
       "c) Multimodel SAR with confidence intervals", 
     confInt = TRUE)

#Barplot of the information criterion weights of each model 
plot(fit_avg, type = "bar", ModTitle = "b) Model weights", cex.lab = 1.3)



# Plot 1: Just the Multi-Model curve with its Confidence Intervals
plot(fit_avg, 
     allCurves = FALSE,            # Hide individual models
     confInt   = TRUE,             # Show the bootstrapped CI polygon
     pcol      = "darkblue",
     ModTitle  = "a) ISAR with 95% CI")

# Plot 2: All individual models + the Multi-Model curve separated on top
plot(fit_avg, 
     mmSep     = TRUE,             # Draws the multi-model curve distinctly
     pcol      = "gray50",
     ModTitle  = "b) Underlying Models")

# Plot 3: Barplot of Information Criterion Weights (Akaike Weights)
plot(fit_avg, 
     type      = "bar",            # Switches plot type to a bar chart
     ModTitle  = "c) Model AICc Weights", 
     cex.lab   = 1.2)

# Reset graphical parameters to default
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

> 1.  Look at the `summary()` output under the section
>     `Models that failed to fit or pass checks`. Which models were
>     excluded, and what was the specific reason (Normality,
>     Homogeneity, or Convergence)?
>
> 2.  Compare the cumulative weight of Asymptotic models vs.
>     Continuous-acceleration models (like the Power model). Does the
>     flora of the Aegean islands show signs of "carrying capacity
>     saturation" (asymptotic behavior), or does richness increase
>     indefinitely with island area?

## GLMM - Model average

One major caveat of the above approach is that it only accounts for the
effect of area on diversity, while we know that many other abiotic
variables can influence the patterns of species diversity and
distribution in space and time. To account for this, we can create a
Generalized Linear Mixed Model (GLMM) with all the abiotic predictors as
fixed effects and then perform model averaging to identify the most
important predictors of taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity in our
dataset. We could use each island's biogeographical regionn as a random
effect, but let's leave that for another time[^2].

[^2]: Or you could try it at home. This is highly recommended if the
    data consists of one observation per island, but the islands belong
    to distinct, historically or spatially cohesive groups (e.g.,
    categorical clusters derived from taxonomic or phylogenetic turnover
    matrices, such as the ones we're going to create). Using a
    categorical bioregion assignment as a random intercept accounts for
    spatial autocorrelation and shared evolutionary history. It tells
    the model: "Islands within the same cluster share a regional species
    pool and unmeasured historical contingencies, so their baselines
    (intercepts) will be more similar to each other than to islands in
    different clusters."

In the past, researchers used to perform model selection with
multivariate regression models, best subset regression, stepwise
regression, etc., but these methods have been criticised for their
tendency to overfit the data and produce unreliable results.

So we're going to use the `MuMIn` 1.46.0 R package to perform model
averaging, which is a more robust method for identifying the most
important predictors of diversity in our dataset.

```{r GLMM, eval = F}
##============================================================================##
## GLMM - Model average ----
##============================================================================##

##============================================================================##
## set na.action for dredge() to work globally ----
##============================================================================##
options(na.action = "na.fail")
##============================================================================##

##============================================================================##
## Define all the response variables we want to run -----
##============================================================================##
response_vars <- c("PD", "SR", "WE", "PE")
##============================================================================##


##============================================================================##
## Run the workflow over all variables automatically ----
##============================================================================##
all_results <- purrr::map(
  setNames(response_vars, response_vars), 
  ~ run_mumin_workflow(
    data           = srdf, 
    response_var   = .x, 
    predictor_vars = aegean_predictors
  )
)
##============================================================================##
```

```{r load-slow-file-mumin, include = FALSE, cache = TRUE, eval = T}
all_results <- readRDS('RDS/GLMM results.rds')
```

Let's see what we got. The `extract_pub_table` function creates a nice
publication table with the estimates, standard errors, confidence
intervals and relative importance of each predictor in the averaged
model, while the `create_forest_plot` function creates a forest plot for
the same model[^3].

[^3]: You can check the code of these and all other functions in the
    `Several functions.R` script, but they are pretty straightforward.
    The first one uses the `broom` package to tidy the model output and
    the second one uses `ggplot2` to create the forest plot.

> Remember that a predictor is considered important if its confidence
> intervals do not overlap with zero and if it has a high relative
> importance (e.g., \> 0.7).

```{r slow-function-extract, include = FALSE, cache = TRUE, eval = T}
extract_pub_table <- function(model_results) {
  # 1. Summarize the averaged model
  avg_sum <- summary(model_results$averaged_model)
  
  # 2. Extract the 'full' coefficients matrix 
  coefs <- as.data.frame(avg_sum$coefmat.full) %>%
    rownames_to_column("Variable")
  
  # 3. Extract 95% Confidence Intervals
  cis <- as.data.frame(confint(model_results$averaged_model, full = TRUE)) %>%
    rownames_to_column("Variable") %>%
    rename(CI_Lower = `2.5 %`, CI_Upper = `97.5 %`)
  
  # 4. Extract Variable Importance
  importances <- data.frame(
    Variable = names(model_results$importance),
    Importance = as.numeric(model_results$importance)
  )
  
  # 5. Combine everything into a final table and clean it up
  pub_table <- coefs %>%
    left_join(cis, by = "Variable") %>%
    left_join(importances, by = "Variable") %>%
    # Select and rename the columns
    select(
      Variable,
      Estimate,
      Std_Error = `Std. Error`,
      CI_Lower,
      CI_Upper,
      P_value = `Pr(>|z|)`,
      Importance
    ) %>%
    # Round all numeric columns to 3 decimal places
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
    # Sort from most important variable to least important
    arrange(desc(Importance))
  
  return(pub_table)
}


create_forest_plot <- function(pub_table, plot_title = "Model-Averaged Predictors") {
  
  # 1. Prep the data for plotting
  plot_data <- pub_table %>%
    # Remove the Intercept
    filter(Variable != "(Intercept)") %>%
    # Create a new column to identify "Significant" variables (CI doesn't cross zero)
    mutate(
      Significant = ifelse(CI_Lower > 0 | CI_Upper < 0, "Significant", "Not Significant"),
      # Lock in the order of the variables so the most important are at the top
      Variable = factor(Variable, levels = rev(Variable))
    )
  
  # 2. Build the Forest Plot
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Estimate, y = Variable, color = Significant)) +
    # Draw the critical "Line of No Effect" at zero
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 1) +
    
    # Draw the Confidence Intervals (horizontal lines)
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = CI_Lower, xmax = CI_Upper), height = 0.2, linewidth = 0.8) +
    
    # Draw the point estimates (the dots)
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    
    # Customize the colors 
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Not Significant" = "gray70", "Significant" = "#005b96")) +
    
    # Clean, professional theme
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), 
      axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", color = "black"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_blank()
    ) +
    
    # Labels
    labs(
      x = "Model-Averaged Estimate (95% CI)",
      y = NULL,
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = "Relative variable importance determines order (top to bottom)"
    )
  
  # Return the ggplot object
  return(p)
}
```

```{r GLLM2, eval = T}
##============================================================================##

##============================================================================##

##============================================================================##

```

> Check the top models, the summary and the relative importance for the
> other response variables

> **Conceptual Note: "Dredging" vs. A Priori Model Selection**
>
> In this workshop, we use the `MuMIn` package to perform an
> "all-subsets" model selection (via the `dredge()` function). This is a
> highly exploratory approach, ideal when we want to screen multiple
> environmental variables and calculate their relative importance
> ($\Sigma w_i$).
>
> However, if your research is driven by very specific, competing
> ecological theories (e.g., you want to strictly compare a
> "Climate-only" hypothesis against an "Isolation-only" hypothesis), you
> should NOT use `dredge()`. Instead, you should manually construct only
> those specific models and compare them. In R, packages like
> `AICcmodavg` are explicitly designed for this type of strict *a
> priori* hypothesis testing.
>
> **Rule of thumb:** Use `MuMIn` when exploring which variables matter.
> Use `AICcmodavg` when testing specific, pre-defined theories.

### The "Golden Rule" of Confidence Intervals

When looking at regression coefficients (your **Estimate**), the 95%
Confidence Interval tells you the range where we are 95% sure the *true*
effect lies.

The most important thing to look for is **whether the interval crosses
zero** (i.e., the `CI_Lower` is negative and the `CI_Upper` is
positive):

-   **If it DOES NOT cross zero:** The effect is robust and consistent.
    We are confident in the direction of the relationship (either
    strictly positive or strictly negative).

-   **If it DOES cross zero:** The effect is uncertain. Because the true
    effect could plausibly be positive, negative, or exactly zero, we
    cannot confidently conclude that this variable drives a consistent
    change in your response variable.

# Beta diversity

## Taxonomic beta diversity

We will compute taxonomic and phylogenetic beta diversity and their
components using the betapart 1.6.1 R package
[@baselga_textlesstttextgreaterbetaparttextlesstttextgreater_2012]. More
specifically, for both Taxonomic Beta Diversity (TBD) and Phylogenetic
Beta Diversity (PBD), overall dissimilarity (Sørensen index, β_sor) was
partitioned into its turnover (Simpson index, β_sim) and
nestedness-resultant (β_sne) components. All subsequent macroecological
and biogeographical analyses focus on β_sim, as it is a metric
well-suited for bioregionalization analyses, since it’s insensitive to
interregional richness differences [@baselga_partitioning_2010;
@kreft_contrasting_2010].

To distinguish true spatial turnover from artifacts caused by richness
gradients (alpha diversity differences), we should have constructed null
models for TBD by applying the conservative independent swap algorithm
for 999 matrix permutations, which preserves both site richness (row
sums) and species occurrence frequencies (column sums), using the
`randomizeMatrix` function from the `picante` 1.8.2 R package and then
calculate the Standardized Effect Sizes (SES) and significance
(p-values) of pairwise turnover. If anyone is interested doing that,
feel free to contact me to provide the relevant R code.

```{r taxonomic-bd, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Compute OBSERVED taxonomic beta diversity ----
##============================================================================##
obs_beta <- betapart::beta.pair(comm_dense, index.family = "sorensen")

# Extract as numeric vectors (one value per pairwise comparison)
obs_sor <- as.numeric(obs_beta$beta.sor)   # Total Sørensen dissimilarity
obs_sim <- as.numeric(obs_beta$beta.sim)   # Turnover (Simpson)
obs_sne <- as.numeric(obs_beta$beta.sne)   # Nestedness-resultant

obs_sim_dist <- obs_beta$beta.sim
obs_sor_dist <- obs_beta$beta.sor
obs_sne_dist <- obs_beta$beta.sne

## Save it to disk if you want by removing the #
# saveRDS(obs_sor_dist, 'RDS/Taxonomic_observed_sorensen.rds')
# saveRDS(obs_sim_dist, 'RDS/Taxonomic_observed_simpson.rds')
# saveRDS(obs_sne_dist, 'RDS/Taxonomic_observed_nestedness.rds')
##============================================================================##
```

## Phylogenetic beta diversity

PBD will be calculated using the function `phylobeta` from the
`phyloregion` 1.0.9 R package [@daru_phyloregion_2020;
@daru_endemism_2020; @daru_understanding_2017].

To ensure robustness, pairwise phylogenetic distances should be computed
across at least 100 phylogenetic trees, and the mean pairwise distances
should be extracted to form the final PBD matrices. Due to time
constraints, this will not be done here and now, but a relevant R script
is provided for anyone interested in running this type of analysis.

```{r phylogenetic-bd, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Calculate the phylogenetic beta diversity ----
##============================================================================##
obs_pbd <- phyloregion::phylobeta(comm_sparse, 
                                  phy,
                                  index = "sorensen")

# Extract as numeric vectors (one value per pairwise comparison)
obs_sor_pbd <- as.numeric(obs_pbd$phylo.beta.sor)   # Total Sørensen dissimilarity
obs_sim_pbd <- as.numeric(obs_pbd$phylo.beta.sim)   # Turnover (Simpson)
obs_sne_pbd <- as.numeric(obs_pbd$phylo.beta.sne)   # Nestedness-resultant

obs_sim_pbd_dist <- obs_pbd$phylo.beta.sim
obs_sor_pbd_dist <- obs_pbd$hylo.beta.sor
obs_sne_pbd_dist <- obs_pbd$phylo.beta.sne

## Save it to disk if you want by removing the #
# saveRDS(obs_sor_pbd_dist, 'RDS/Phylogenetic_observed_sorensen.rds')
# saveRDS(obs_sim_pbd_dist, 'RDS/Phylogenetic_observed_simpson.rds')
# saveRDS(obs_sne_pbd_dist, 'RDS/Phylogenetic_observed_nestedness.rds')
##============================================================================##
```

## Reload distance matrices

```{r reload-distances}
##============================================================================##

tax_sim   <- readRDS('RDS/Taxonomic_observed_simpson.rds') 
##============================================================================##
```

```{r load-slow-file, include = FALSE, cache = TRUE, eval = T}
tax_sim   <- readRDS('RDS/Taxonomic_observed_simpson.rds') 
```

```{r reload-attr, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Ensure labels are perfectly aligned ----

attr(phylo_sim, "Labels") <- plants$Island

```

# Hierarchical clustering

## Linkage selection (cophenetic correlation)

Hierarchical clustering nests sites into groups, but the result depends
entirely on the linkage rule — i.e., how distance between two clusters
is defined once they start merging.

To select the linkage algorithm best representing the floristic
divergences among islands without imposing a particular hierarchical
structure a priori, we will test various commonly applied hierarchical
clustering algorithms on each turnover-component dissimilarity matrix
using the function `hclust` of the `stats` 4.5.3 R package (R Core Team
2026):

-   **Ward's minimum-variance criterion** (Ward's D and Ward's D₂),
-   **single linkage**,
-   **complete linkage**,
-   **unweighted pair-group method with arithmetic mean** (UPGMA),
-   **unweighted pair-group method using centroids** (UPGMC) and
-   **weighted pair-group method with arithmetic mean** (WPGMA),

following Kreft and Jetz (2010) and Holt et al. (2013).

For each dendrogram, we will compute the cophenetic correlation
coefficient (Sokal and Rohlf 1962) as the Pearson correlation between
the original pairwise dissimilarities and the cophenetic distances
extracted from the dendrogram (i.e., the heights at which any two leaves
are first joined), using the `cophenetic` function of the stats 4.5.3 R
package (R Core Team, 2026).

Conceptually, this coefficient quantifies the extent to which the
dendrogram preserves the metric structure of the input dissimilarity
matrix, with values closer to 1 indicating less topological distortion.

The linkage method yielding the highest cophenetic correlation will be
retained for all downstream analyses, providing an objective,
distortion-minimising basis for the dendrogram topology rather than a
choice based on convention or visual inspection.

So, `evaluate_linkage()` fits eight standard rules (ward.D, ward.D2,
single, complete, average, mcquitty, median, centroid) and asks: how
faithful is each resulting tree to the original pairwise distances?

For each method we compute the cophenetic correlation — the Pearson
correlation between:

-   the original distances and

-   the heights at which each pair of sites is first joined in the
    dendrogram.

Again, a value near 1 means the tree preserves the input distances
almost perfectly. The method with the **highest** cophenetic correlation
is the best choice for hierarchical clustering.

Note that this is not a test of statistical significance, but a way to
choose the most faithful representation of the original distances.

```{r linkage-selection, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Choose the best linkage method with evaluate_linkage() ----
##============================================================================##
linkage_phylo <- evaluate_linkage(phylo_sim)
linkage_phylo

linkage_tax   <- evaluate_linkage(tax_sim)
linkage_tax

## We pick the "winner" method for each matrix and save it for later use in the
## clustering step
link_method <- "average" ## Same method for both matrices for easier comparison

hc_phylo <- hclust(phylo_sim, method = link_method)
hc_tax   <- hclust(tax_sim,   method = link_method)

# These two hclust objects are the trees we will cut, evaluate, and visualise.
##============================================================================##
```

## Optimal number of regions (KGS)

Once we have a tree we still need to decide where to cut it. Cutting too
high gives one mega-region; cutting too low gives one cluster per
island.

We use the KGS (Kelley–Gardner–Sutcliffe) penalty from the `maptree`
package, which balances two opposing criteria:

-   the within-cluster spread (penalised when clusters are
    heterogeneous, i.e. cutting too high) and

-   the between-cluster cost (penalised when many clusters are very
    similar, i.e. cutting too low).

The optimal K **minimises** the sum of both penalties.

We will turn this into a publication-ready plot in `plot_kgs()` later.

```{r optimal-k, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Find the optimal number of regions with find_optimal_k() ----
##============================================================================##
opt_phylo <- find_optimal_k(hc_phylo, phylo_sim)
opt_phylo$optimal_k
opt_phylo$kgs_df

opt_tax   <- find_optimal_k(hc_tax, tax_sim)
opt_tax$optimal_k
opt_tax$kgs_df
```

## Silhouettes

What `silhouette()` does?

For every site is the mean distance from to sites in the nearest other
cluster.

-   Values near +1 mean the site is well inside its region

-   values near 0 mean it sits on a boundary

-   negative values mean the site would actually fit better in a
    neighbouring region.

You see a matrix with one row per island (cluster ID, neighbour cluster,
silhouette width).

The `summary()` reports the mean silhouette per cluster and overall.

We will later plot the per-island bars with `plot_silhouette()`.

```{r cut-silhouette, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Cut the tree and compute silhouettes ----
##============================================================================##
clusters_phylo <- cutree(hc_phylo, k = opt_phylo$optimal_k)
clusters_tax   <- cutree(hc_tax,   k = opt_tax$optimal_k)

sil_phylo <- silhouette(clusters_phylo, phylo_sim)
sil_tax   <- silhouette(clusters_tax,   tax_sim)

summary(sil_phylo)
summary(sil_tax)
```

# Statistical validation

Hierarchical clustering will always hand back a partition, even from
random noise. So we need to test whether the partition is statistically
and practically meaningful. The function runs four complementary checks:

-   **NMDS** (`vegan::metaMDS`). Non-metric multidimensional scaling
    projects the 48 islands into 2-D so we can see whether islands in
    the same cluster sit close together. The reported stress tells us
    how much the 2-D projection distorts the original distances (\< 0.10
    excellent, 0.10–0.20 fair, \> 0.20 poor).

-   **PERMANOVA** (`vegan::adonis2`). A permutational MANOVA testing the
    null hypothesis: the mean compositional centroid is identical across
    clusters. A small p (\< 0.05) means clusters truly differ in
    composition; the reported R\^2 tells us how much variance the
    partition explains.

-   **β-dispersion** (`vegan::betadisper + permutest`). Tests whether
    clusters differ in their internal heterogeneity. This is a sanity
    check for PERMANOVA: if dispersions differ a lot, a *significant*
    PERMANOVA could be picking up spread rather than centroid
    differences.

-   **Cluster stability** (f`pc::clusterboot)`. Bootstraps the data 999
    times, re-clusters each replicate, and reports — for every cluster —
    its mean Jaccard similarity to its bootstrap counterpart.

Rule of thumb: `> 0.75 stable`, `0.60–0.75 cautious`, `< 0.60 unstable`.

No plot is drawn here, but the returned object contains everything ready
to plot:

-   `val_phylo$nmds_df` (tidy NMDS coordinates)

\-`val_phylo$nmds_stress`,

-   `val_phylo$permanova`,

-   `val_phylo$dispersion`, and

-   `val_phylo$stability` (one Jaccard mean per cluster).

We turn the NMDS into a panel with later.

```{r validation, eval = T, results = 'hide', message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
##============================================================================##
## Statistical validation with validate_bioregion() ----
##============================================================================##
val_phylo <- validate_bioregion(phylo_sim, clusters_phylo,
                                hclust_method = link_method,
                                k             = opt_phylo$optimal_k)

val_tax   <- validate_bioregion(tax_sim, clusters_tax,
                                hclust_method = link_method,
                                k             = opt_tax$optimal_k)
```

```{r nmds, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## See the results ----
##============================================================================##
val_tax$nmds_stress
val_tax$permanova
val_tax$stability
```

# Indicator Species Analysis

A bioregion is more than a clustering label — biologically, we want to
know which species characterise each region.

ISA (`indicspecies::multipatt` with the point-biserial-correlation
variant r.g) tests, for every species, whether it is over-represented in
one cluster (or combination of clusters) relative to the rest, and gives
a permutation p-value.

In other words, an indicator species analysis (ISA) is used to identify
any taxa that could distinguish each cluster by estimating Pearson's phi
coefficient of association, corrected for differences in group size
using the function `multipatt` from the indicspecies 1.8.0 R package.

isa_phylo is a data frame with one row per species:

-   the cluster (or combination of clusters) it indicates,

-   an association strength (stat), and

-   p-value.

Filtering on p.value `<= 0.05` gives the diagnostic-species list —
exactly what you would put in a regional floristic table.

> This analysis is too time-consuming for this specific dataset, so we
> won't run it here, but the code is provided for anyone interested in
> running it on their own or this dataset.

```{r isa}
##============================================================================##
## Indicator Species Analysis ----
##============================================================================##
isa_phylo <- run_isa(comm, clusters_phylo)
summary(isa_phylo)

isa_tax   <- run_isa(comm, clusters_tax)
summary(isa_tax)
```

# The `bioregion` ecosystem

## Convert distances to bioregion format

The `bioregion package` does not accept a base-R dist object; it needs a
long data frame with three columns (Site1, Site2, value) and the S3
class `bioregion.pairwise.metric`.

The function:

-   flattens the lower triangle of the matrix,

-   attaches the class plus the type = "dissimilarity" attribute, and

-   returns the data frame

You see a tibble with with Site1, Site2, Simpson.

No new analysis happens here — but every downstream `bioregion::*` call
needs this object.

```{r convert-bioregion, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Convert to the bioregion-package format with convert_dist_to_bioregion() ----
##============================================================================##
dissim_phylo_br <- convert_dist_to_bioregion(phylo_sim, metric_name = "Simpson")
dissim_tax_br   <- convert_dist_to_bioregion(tax_sim,   metric_name = "Simpson")

head(dissim_phylo_br)
```

## Hierarchical clustering inside `bioregion`

It is essentially the same UPGMA we ran in the first step, but inside
the `bioregion` ecosystem so the result inherits the
`bioregion.clusters` class and is recognised by the package's downstream
tools (network metrics, contribution metrics, comparison utilities).

We feed the same link_method and the same K we already validated, so the
partition is identical to `clusters_phylo` / `clusters_tax`. We just
need it in bioregion format for the next step.

```{r bioregion-hclust, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Hierarchical clustering inside the bioregion framework with hclu_hierarclust() ----
##============================================================================##
hier_phylo <- hclu_hierarclust(dissim_phylo_br,
                               index   = "Simpson",
                               method  = link_method,
                               n_clust = opt_phylo$optimal_k)

hier_tax   <- hclu_hierarclust(dissim_tax_br,
                               index   = "Simpson",
                               method  = link_method,
                               n_clust = opt_tax$optimal_k)
##============================================================================##
```

## Region-level metrics

For each region this function computes summary metrics describing the
region's biotic identity:

-   **n_sites** — how many islands belong to it

-   **n_species** — total species richness across those islands

-   **end_species** — species found only in that region (regional
    endemics within our pool)

-   **end_richness** — proportion of regional species that are exclusive
    to it (the endemism rate)

-   **rho**: the coherence metric of Lenormand et al.
    [-@lenormand_biogeographical_2019]: how strongly species are
    associated with the region versus with the rest of the network.
    Higher p = more cohesive, biologically distinct region

You see a small data frame with one row per region. These rows go
straight into the results table for any paper you might want to publish.

```{r bioregion-metrics, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Region-level descriptive metrics with bioregion_metrics_fixed() ----
##============================================================================##

## Ensure that the community matrix has the island names
rownames(comm_sparse) <- hier_phylo$clusters$ID

metrics_phylo <- bioregion_metrics_fixed(bioregionalization = hier_phylo,
                                         comat              = comm_sparse %>% sparse2dense,
                                         map                = aegean_islands %>% 
                                           dplyr::mutate(ID = 1:48), 
                                         col_bioregion      = 1)
metrics_phylo

metrics_tax   <- bioregion_metrics_fixed(bioregionalization = hier_tax,
                                         comat              = comm_sparse %>% sparse2dense,
                                         map                = aegean_islands %>% 
                                           dplyr::mutate(ID = 1:48), 
                                         col_bioregion      = 1)
metrics_tax
```

## Island-level affiliation

A clustering label is binary — "this island is in region 2" — but
biologically that is an oversimplification. Some peaks are deep in their
region's core, others are near a boundary and could plausibly belong to
a neighbouring region.

So, we will quantify the affiliation strength of each Aegean island to
its assigned biogeographical region or cluster using a modified version
of the `calc_affiliation_evoreg` function from the
[Herodotools](https://gabrielnakamura.github.io/Herodotools/) 2.0.1 R
package.

-   Values approaching 1 indicate strong affiliation with a single
    region

-   Values near 0 denote transitional characteristics between regions

You see a small data frame with one row per island and an affiliation
column. This is the variable we will use to colour the affiliation map.
Islands painted in deep colours are strongholds so to speak; pale ones
are transition peaks — biogeographically the most interesting cases.

```{r affiliation, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Island-level affiliation with calc_affiliation_evoreg_fixed() ----
##============================================================================##
afi_phylo <- calc_affiliation_evoreg_fixed(phylo.comp.dist = phylo_sim,
                                           groups          = factor(clusters_phylo))

afi_tax   <- calc_affiliation_evoreg_fixed(phylo.comp.dist = tax_sim,
                                           groups          = factor(clusters_tax))

head(afi_phylo)
```

# Figures

## Region colours

A bioregion analysis only "reads" if the same colour is used for the
same cluster in every panel — dendrogram, map, KGS curve, silhouette
bars, NMDS ellipses, affiliation map.

`get_palette()` is a thin wrapper around the requested `ggsci` palette
function (npg, aaas, lancet, nejm, …).

Given a number of clusters k, it returns a named character vector of hex
colours of length k, with names equal to "1", "2", …, "k".

By having the names match the cluster IDs returned by `cutree()`, every
downstream plot can do `scale_*_manual(values = pal)` and the colour
assignment is automatic and consistent.

```{r palettes, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Generate region colours with get_palette() ----
##============================================================================##
pal_phylo <- get_palette(k = opt_phylo$optimal_k, scheme = 'npg')
pal_tax   <- get_palette(k = opt_tax$optimal_k,   scheme = 'npg')

pal_phylo
pal_tax
```

## Build the spatial bioregion objects

`clusters_phylo` is a named integer vector (names = island names, values
= cluster IDs).

We pull the cluster ID for every polygon, convert it to a factor (so
ggplot2 legends behave), and attach the matching hex colour for
convenience.

The result is an sf object with two new columns

You see a spatial data frame with one row per island, with cluster and
color columns appended.

```{r bioregion-sf, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Join clusters back to the shapefile to build bioregion_sf ----
##============================================================================##
bioregion_sf_phylo <- aegean_islands %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(cluster = factor(clusters_phylo[as.character(Island)]),
                color   = pal_phylo[as.character(cluster)])

bioregion_sf_tax <- aegean_islands %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(cluster = factor(clusters_tax[as.character(Island)]),
                color   = pal_tax[as.character(cluster)])
##============================================================================##
```

## Cophenetic correlations

```{r cophenetic, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Manually compute the correlation ----
##============================================================================##
r_coph_phylo <- cor(cophenetic(hc_phylo), phylo_sim)
r_coph_tax   <- cor(cophenetic(hc_tax),   tax_sim)
##============================================================================##
```

## Assemble the `res_*` lists

Now we assemble the `res_*` lists in the same shape the wrapper would
have returned, so every `plot_*` function can read from them unchanged:

```{r dend-slow-file, include = FALSE, cache = TRUE, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Align colours with the dendrogram leaves with build_dend_data() ----
##============================================================================##
dend_phylo <- build_dend_data(hc  = hc_phylo,
                              k   = clusters_phylo,
                              pal = pal_phylo)

dend_tax   <- build_dend_data(hc  = hc_tax,
                              k   = clusters_tax,
                              pal = pal_tax)

str(dend_phylo, max.level = 1)
```

```{r res-lists, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Assembly the res_* lists ----
##============================================================================##
tax_pal      <- get_palette(opt_tax$optimal_k)
tax_dend_dat <- build_dend_data(hc_tax, opt_tax$optimal_k, tax_pal)

res_phylo <- list(
  dist_mat     = phylo_sim,
  hc           = hc_phylo,
  r_coph       = r_coph_phylo,
  optimal_k    = opt_phylo$optimal_k,
  kgs_df       = opt_phylo$kgs_df,
  clusters     = clusters_phylo,
  silhouette   = sil_phylo,
  palette      = pal_phylo,
  dend_data    = dend_phylo,
  bioregion_sf = bioregion_sf_phylo,
  id_col       = "Island"
)

res_tax <- list(
  dist_mat     = tax_sim,
  pal_aligned  = dend_tax$pal_aligned,
  ggd          = tax_dend_dat$ggd,
  hc           = hc_tax,
  r_coph       = r_coph_tax,
  optimal_k    = opt_tax$optimal_k,
  kgs_df       = opt_tax$kgs_df,
  clusters     = clusters_tax,
  silhouette   = sil_tax,
  palette      = pal_tax,
  dend_data    = dend_tax,
  bioregion_sf = bioregion_sf_tax,
  id_col       = "Island"
)
##============================================================================##
```

## Dendrograms, KGS, Silhouette and a map

### Dendrogram

`plot_dendroram` reads `res$dend_data$segments` to draw the branches
with `geom_segment()`, then `res$dend_data$labels_df` to draw the italic
island names with `geom_text()`, with horizontal alignment chosen so the
labels sit just past the leaves.

The y-axis is the β_sim merging height. The cophenetic correlation
`r_coph` is annotated in the top-right corner via
`annotate("text", …, label = paste("r =", round(res$r_coph, 3)))`.

You see a horizontal dendrogram in which each clade is painted in its
region's colour, internal grey branches mark the merges between regions,
and the height at which two clades fuse is the β_sim dissimilarity at
which those island groups become indistinguishable.

The annotated `r_coph` tells them how faithfully the tree preserves the
original distances — values above 0.75 are good, above 0.85 excellent.

## Coloured dendrogram data

A hclust object stores merges in merge order, but cutree() labels are in
original site order, and ggplot reads dendrograms in visual leaf order
from left to right. If we naively colour leaves by `clusters[i]` we get
a chromatic catastrophe. `build_dend_data()` resolves this by:

-   Calling `dendextend::as.dendrogram(hc)` and walking the leaves to
    recover the left-to-right leaf order.

-   Re-ordering clusters to that order, then mapping each leaf to its
    colour via `palette[as.character(clusters)]`.

-   Colouring branches: each internal branch is painted with the cluster
    colour if all its descendants belong to the same cluster, else grey.
    Done with `dendextend::color_branches()` / `set("branches_col", …)`.

-   Returning a list with at least: `dend` (the coloured dendrogram
    object), `segments` (a data frame produced by
    `ggdendro::dendro_data()` for ggplot2), `labels_df` (a data frame
    with x, y, label, cluster, color for every leaf — used to draw the
    italic island names in the right colour).

```{r dendrogram-data, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Align colours with the dendrogram leaves with build_dend_data() ----
##============================================================================##
dend_phylo <- build_dend_data(hc  = hc_phylo,
                              k   = clusters_phylo,
                              pal = pal_phylo)

dend_tax   <- build_dend_data(hc  = hc_tax,
                              k   = clusters_tax,
                              pal = pal_tax)
```

### KGS

`plot_kgs` plots `res$kgs_df$k` on the x-axis and `res$kgs_df$penalty`
on the y-axis as a `geom_line()` with `geom_point()`.

The optimal K is highlighted with a larger filled point in the cluster's
own colour (`pal[as.character(optimal_k)]`) and labelled via
`geom_label_repel()`.

You see a U-shaped (or hockey-stick) curve.

The minimum corresponds to the K that best balances within-cluster
homogeneity and between-cluster distinctness.

The highlighted point is the chosen partition. If the curve is very flat
near the minimum, several Ks are roughly equivalent and your choice is
robust; a sharply pointed minimum means the optimal K is unambiguous.

### Silhouette

`plot_silhouette` converts `res$silhouette` (a `cluster::silhouette`
object) into a tidy data frame with one row per island (island, cluster,
sil_width, neighbour), sorts rows by cluster then descending silhouette
width, and draws horizontal geom_col() bars filled with pal.

A dashed grey horizontal line marks the mean silhouette, annotated
numerically.

You see one bar per island, grouped by region and colour-matched.

-   Tall bars (close to +1) = well-classified islands, deep in their
    region.

-   Short or negative bars = islands sitting on a boundary or arguably
    misclassified.

Compare the mean silhouette:

-   `>= 0.50` strong,
-   `0.25 – 0.50` acceptable,
-   `<= 0.25 weak` partition.

### Map

`plot_map` uses `geom_sf(data = res$bioregion_sf, aes(fill = cluster))`
plus `scale_fill_manual(values = res$palette)` to paint every polygon in
its region's colour.

Adds island labels with `geom_sf_text()` (or
`ggrepel::geom_text_repel()` with `stat = "sf_coordinates"`).

You see the Aegean basin painted in coloured patches. Spatially
contiguous patches mean a region is geographically coherent (e.g.,
Cyclades sticking together). Scattered same-coloured polygons mean two
distant islands share an ecological identity that is not explained by
proximity — a much more interesting biogeographical story.

```{r preview-tax, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Generate aesthetic data ----
##============================================================================##
tax_pal      <- get_palette(opt_tax$optimal_k)
tax_dend_dat <- build_dend_data(hc_tax, opt_tax$optimal_k, tax_pal)

# Package everything into a list for the plotting wrappers
res_tax <- list(
  ggd          = tax_dend_dat$ggd, 
  pal_aligned  = tax_dend_dat$pal_aligned,
  r_coph       = linkage_tax$cophenetic_r[1],
  kgs_df       = opt_tax$kgs_df, 
  optimal_k    = opt_tax$optimal_k,
  palette      = tax_pal,
  sil          = sil_tax,
  bioregion_sf = aegean_islands %>%
    mutate(color = tax_dend_dat$pal_aligned[as.character(clusters_tax)])
)

# Render the plots
p_dend_tax <- plot_dendrogram(res_tax,  tag = "(a)")
p_kgs_tax  <- plot_kgs(res_tax,         tag = "(b)")
p_sil_tax  <- plot_silhouette(res_tax,  tag = "(c)")
p_map_tax  <- plot_map(res_tax,         tag = "(d)")

p_dend_tax

p_kgs_tax

p_sil_tax

p_map_tax

# Composite figure - I won't plot it here
# (p_dend_tax | p_map_tax) / (p_kgs_tax | p_sil_tax) + 
#   plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1))
##============================================================================##
```

## NMDS

To visualise the pairwise floristic relationships among the Aegean
islands, we projected each turnover-component dissimilarity matrix into
a two-dimensional space using non-metric multidimensional scaling
(NMDS), implemented through the `metaMDS` function of the vegan 2.7.3 R
package [@oksanen_vegan_2018].

Here we read `val$nmds_df`(NMDS coordinates produced by `metaMDS()`
inside `validate_bioregion()`), draw points coloured by region, add
repelled island labels, and overlay 95 % confidence ellipses per cluster
with `stat_ellipse(type = "norm", level = 0.95)`. The stress value is
annotated bottom-right.

You see a 2-D scatter of the Aegean islands in compositional space.

Tight, well-separated coloured ellipses validate the partition.
Overlapping ellipses warn that, although the dendrogram cut yields
distinct clusters, the multivariate cloud does not really separate them.

The stress tells them how trustworthy this 2-D view is:

-   `<= 0.10` excellent,
-   `0.10–0.20` fair,
-   `>= 0.20` don't over-interpret distances on the plot

```{r plot-nmds, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## plot_nmds() ----
##============================================================================##
p_nmds_phylo <- ggplot(val_phylo$nmds_df,
                       aes(x = NMDS1, 
                           y = NMDS2, 
                           colour = Cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = Mountain),
                           size        = 3, 
                           show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_ellipse(level    = 0.95, 
               linetype = 2,
               alpha    = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = res_phylo$palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title    = paste("NMDS:", "PBD"),
       subtitle = paste("Stress =", round(val_phylo$nmds_stress, 3)))

p_nmds_phylo

p_nmds_tax <- ggplot(val_tax$nmds_df,
                     aes(x = NMDS1, 
                         y = NMDS2, 
                         colour = Cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = Mountain),
                           size        = 3, 
                           show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_ellipse(level    = 0.95, 
               linetype = 2,
               alpha    = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = res_tax$palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title    = paste("NMDS:", "TBD"),
       subtitle = paste("Stress =", round(val_tax$nmds_stress, 3)))
p_nmds_tax
```

## Affiliation maps

Please note that the `create_vector_map` function is very time-consuming
as it uses very high resolution altitudinal raster data. If you want to
run this code, consider using reducing the resolution of the altitudinal
raster data in the function body of `create_vector_map`[^4].

[^4]: You can find it in the `Several functions.R` file, which
    admittedly is a bit chaotic

```{r plot-affiliation}
##============================================================================##

shape_aff_phylo <- res_phylo$bioregion_sf %>%
  dplyr::left_join(
    tibble::rownames_to_column(as.data.frame(afi_phylo), "Island"),

p_aff_phylo <- create_vector_map(

p_aff_phylo

p_aff_tax <- create_vector_map(

)

p_aff_tax

##============================================================================##
```

```{r build-all-bio, eval = T}
bio <- list(
  tax_sim = build_bioregion(tax_sim,   aegean_islands),
  phy_sim = build_bioregion(phylo_sim, aegean_islands)
)
##============================================================================##
```

```{r diag-table, eval = T}
##============================================================================##

diag_table <- tibble(
  Combination = names(bio),
  Optimal_k   = map_int(bio, "optimal_k"),

)

diag_table
```

## Pairwise comparisons of interest

```{r comparisons-tibble, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Define all pairwise comparisons of interest ----
##============================================================================##
comparisons <- tribble(
  ~name1,        ~name2,    ~comparison_type,
  "phylo_sim",   "tax_sim", "Turnover: Phylo vs Tax"
```

## V-measure

We will also evaluate the degree of spatial association between the
resulting bioregionalization schema using: - the V-measure index
[@nowosad_spatial_2018], which evaluates the balance between homogeneity
and completeness in categorical partitions and - local relative
inhomogeneity [@nowosad_spatial_2018], using the `vmeasure_calc`
function from the `sabre` 0.4.3 R package [@nowosad_spatial_2018].

Once more, the `vmeasure_calc` function is extremely slow for our
dataset, so I've provided an `rds` file with the results of the
V-measure calculations for the comparisons of interest. You can load it
with `readRDS()` if you want to skip the calculations and jump straight
to the results.

```{r slow-vmeasure, include = FALSE, cache = TRUE, eval = T}
vmeasure_results <- readRDS("RDS/Vmeasure_results.rds")
sabre_metrics <- readRDS("RDS/SABRE_metrics.rds")
```

```{r vmeasure, eval = F}
##============================================================================##
## Run V-measure for every comparison ----
##============================================================================##
vmeasure_results <- vmeasure_calc(
  x      = bio$tax_sim$sf,
  y      = bio$phy_sim$sf,
  x_name = group,
  y_name = group
) 

sabre_metrics <- tibble(V_measure       = vmeasure_results$v_measure,
                        Homogeneity     = vmeasure_results$homogeneity,
                        Completeness    = vmeasure_results$completeness,
                        comparison_type = 'TBD vs PBD')

sabre_metrics
```

## Spatial inhomogeneity (rih) maps

```{r rih-maps, eval = T}
##============================================================================##
## Visualise the spatial inhomogeneity (rih) maps for key comparisons ----
##============================================================================##
p_rih1 <- ggplot(vmeasure_results$map1) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = rih), colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = mex.brewer("Revolucion", direction = 1),
                       name   = "rih",
                       limits = c(0, max(vmeasure_results$map1$rih, na.rm = TRUE))) +
  labs(title = "TBD (local inhomogeneity)") +
  theme_minimal()

p_rih2 <- ggplot(vmeasure_results$map2) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = rih), colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = mex.brewer("Revolucion", direction = 1),
                       name   = "rih",
                       limits = c(0, max(vmeasure_results$map2$rih, na.rm = TRUE))) +
  labs(title = "PBD (local inhomogeneity)") +
```
